The eleven ratings for Hellenic Telecom

Hellenic Telecom (OTE): a high-quality, low-risk cash compounder whose 2027 estimates are about to be cut, so the shares are likely to be cheaper to buy after February 2027 than today

Written 29 October 2026, the day before the Q3 2026 results (30 October). Share price 19.03 EUR (27 October); market value about 7.4 bn EUR; two-year-forward P/E 11.1x on consensus EPS and 11.2x on the model's EPS. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Definitions of EBITDA, EPS and free cash flow, and the sources, are in the end notes.

#0Summary: the key insights, implications and conclusions

The conclusion for RichardOTE is a high-quality, low-risk business returning about 8% of its market value in cash each year, but its FY2027 estimates are likely to be cut in February 2027. The better entry point is therefore likely to come after that reset, unless the Q3 call on 30 October names a December 2026 price step of 3.5% or more.

What OTE is. OTE is the cleanest cash-yield case in European telecoms: one country, one currency, no leverage, no minority interests, and a parent (Deutsche Telekom, which owns 54.6%) that wants the cash paid up to it. As Greece's incumbent operator, OTE holds 73% of the Greek telecom EBITDA pool and 93% of the industry's operating free cash flow.

The spine of the case: OTE's core business is flat, and FY2026's growth rests on two supports that move in opposite directions in 2027. The two supports are the contractual price step (2.6% in December 2025) and the EU-funded boom in public information and communications technology (ICT) projects, which lifted System Solutions revenue by 64% in H1 2026 at about a 20% margin. Without those two supports, OTE's gains in fibre and postpaid volumes are absorbed by prepaid erosion, national wholesale decline and Greek cost inflation, leaving the core flat to slightly shrinking. FY2026's guide of +3% EBITDAaL growth, OTE's first explicit numeric guide, was set above consensus and has been held, but it rests on the two supports.

In 2027 the two supports diverge. The December 2026 price step will be bigger than the 2025 step, because Greek inflation in 2026 is running at 3.8% to 5.1%. The public ICT boom will reverse, because the EU's Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), which funds it, ends in December 2026.

Where I differ from the market.

  • The model's FY2027 EBITDAaL growth is +1.0%, against a consensus of about +3%.
  • The model's FY2027 revenue is 6% below consensus, because about half the brokers have not removed the 130 EURm of zero-margin transit revenue that OTE has disclosed it will exit.
  • No broker document says that FY2027 depends on one December price step; my analysis shows that it does.
The next two dated events will probably lower estimates

The FY2027 guide in February 2027 is most likely to be "about +1% to +2%" against the street's +3%, and consensus EPS is likely to be cut by 2% to 3% for FY2027 (from 1.70 EUR) and by 3% to 5% for FY2028. Sell-side sentiment has already softened (the buy share is down 15 points to 54%, Barclays rates the shares Sell, and estimates have been flat for six months), so the market is partly positioned for the cut. However, the next twelve months contain no "beat and raise" event, and even the bull case only holds consensus rather than starting an upgrade cycle. On earnings, OTE therefore fails Richard's test of an unusually positive skew in fundamentals and upgrades.

Where the positive skew does lie: in three places other than earnings.

  1. The multiple, which is set by Greece rather than by the sector. OTE's shares trade with Greece and with their own news: the European telecom basket explains only 4% of the daily variance in OTE's share price. The Greek equity risk premium is falling (Morgan Stanley has cut its estimate from 8% to 7%), MSCI's inclusion of Greece as a Developed Market in May 2027 brings modest net passive inflows, and the sector note records that contractual price rises are "not yet in the Greek price".
  2. The durability of Greek price indexation, which the market underrates. OTE's indexation clause is written into each contract at signing, so it survives the September 2026 Court of Justice ruling. The clause recurs annually, both rivals have applied their own clauses for two rounds, and no Greek authority has challenged it. The market nevertheless groups it with the legal risk to indexation in Germany and Poland.
  3. Capital optionality that is not in the share price. Releveraging to 1.5x EBITDA would add 20% to 25% to EPS, and OTE's 3,800 towers sit in a wholly owned subsidiary that could be monetised. Neither move is under discussion, so neither is priced.

The return: at my fair multiple of 11.5x to 12.0x, the shares return about +19% to +24% to December 2027, and most of that return is cash rather than a bet on re-rating. At the guideline fair multiple of 12.5x, the model gives +28.5% to December 2027 (+23.8% annualised) and +42.5% to June 2029. Split like for like, the return to December 2027 is about 10 points of cash, about 12 points from the multiple rising from 11.2x to 12.5x, and about 6 points from growth in two-year-forward EPS. I set my fair multiple below the guideline (see #11) because the stock has held 12.5x only in years of zero interest rates and double-digit EPS growth, and because the next two catalysts are estimate cuts, not raises. On unchanged earnings, the downside to the five-year trough band of multiples is 8% to 15%, and at the bottom of that band the dividend yield is about 5.5% to 6%.

The return, in one lineThe return is one-third cash, two-fifths re-rating and one-fifth earnings: at Viewforth's fair multiple the cash leg (about 8% a year) is secure, and the re-rating is the upside, not the requirement.

The practical conclusion: prepare to buy after the February 2027 reset rather than today. OTE's fundamentals keep compounding at about 4% a year in EPS and 8% a year in free cash flow per share, while the market's expectations are about to be reset lower. The setup that best fits Richard's criteria (a cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a multiple in the bottom quartile of its history) was crisp in 2025, and the market has since paid for it. That setup is more likely to re-form crisply in the next three to six months, after the February 2027 reset and around MSCI's April 2027 pricing window, than it is to be available today. Three events would make me more positive now, and two would make me negative.

ScoresScorecard of the twelve topics

#1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Key messageThe external forces on OTE net to roughly zero for earnings over the next 18 months and turn slowly negative after 2027; unusually for a European telecom, inflation helps OTE.

Evidence: demand is flat in units but upgrading in value, with high visibility, and all three real headwinds land in 2027.

Two of the headwinds are large. The public ICT surge supplied roughly half of H1 2026's EBITDA growth: System Solutions added 115 to 120 EURm of revenue at an inferred incremental margin of 10% to 20%, against total EBITDAaL growth of about 19 EURm. The Vodafone-PPC venture is the first credible attack on OTE's national wholesale revenue (about 239 EURm in FY2025 at an 80% to 85% margin), which is the layer of the business that carries OTE's excess return.

Inference and so-what. For the next 18 months the price step offsets the ICT and energy headwinds and the first wholesale erosion, so the external forces net to roughly zero for earnings. For 2028 to 2030 they net negative, slowly. Greek inflation, acting through the price clause, is the one external variable that matters for 2027; the speed at which Vodafone, and possibly Nova, migrate their wholesale lines to the venture is the one that matters from 2028. Neither variable is cyclical: both are decisions taken by identifiable parties.

Market view against mine. The market's dominant external debate, PPC's attack on OTE's retail customers, has been settled, and I agree that it is over. PPC has won about 20k customers at a 50% to 59% discount, under 1% of OTE's lines, because PPC offers no mobile and no TV while OTE bundles 70% of its broadband base. The market under-weights the ICT roll-off and over-weights the legal risk to Greek indexation. Deutsche Bank still models ICT growth to 2028, and Morgan Stanley argues that the ICT cliff is exaggerated because only 56% of RRF money had been absorbed by end-2026; my base case, a 15% fall in System Solutions revenue in FY2027, sits between the two houses.

Strongest counter-case. RRF spill-over could keep ICT revenue flat in 2027 while the price step comes in at 4%, giving FY2027 EBITDAaL growth of +3% and leaving consensus intact; I put the probability at about 20%. The spill-over has three possible sources: a one-to-two-year lag in absorbing RRF money, the 23 bn EUR National Development Programme, and a 515 EURm electronic-ID tender with a ten-year maintenance tail.

What would change my view. Q3 2026 System Solutions growth still above +40%, with management no longer calling the surge "front-loaded"; or a Hellenic Competition Commission remedy that caps the venture's open-access pricing.

Score: 50. Tailwinds (fibre migration, regulation, contractual inflation pass-through) and headwinds (the ICT roll-off, energy, a cheaper wholesale network that now has a tenant) balance over 18 months and tilt negative after; this is an average external picture for a European company, with the unusual feature that inflation helps.

#2Internally driven corporate change, and the absence of problems

Key messageThe change programme under the new chief executive was decisive and has delivered its gains; the programme has now matured, and the one internal force still latent is pricing.

Evidence: the change was decisive, and 28 months on its gains are in the numbers. Kostas Nebis became chief executive on 1 July 2024, moving from Deutsche Telekom's bench after a documented turnaround at Hrvatski Telekom, where revenue growth went from -1% to +6%, EBITDAaL growth from -4% to +5% and the payout to 94%.

Inference: OTE is at the "full output" stage of its corporate-change chain, so the benefits already show in the margin, the cash and the share price. The share price is up 25.9% over twelve months on EPS upgrades of about 5%. What remains is execution worth about 1% to 2% of EBITDA a year (voluntary exits, digital deflection, copper switch-off from 2028) and one discrete decision: how much of the FY2026 tax windfall (about 170 EURm of reported cash) goes into the 2027 distribution. In November 2025 the chief executive said that he would smooth the windfall against the 2027 spectrum cost rather than let the distribution spike and then drop; the model's distributions of 585 EURm in 2027 and 600 EURm in 2028 follow that statement.

The problems present are real but modest.

  • Growth has slowed: mobile service revenue growth halved to +2.3% in Q2 2026, and retail fixed revenue growth slowed to +0.3%, as the 2025 rise in the minimum prepaid top-up dropped out of the year-on-year comparison.
  • The quality of growth leans on low-margin public ICT.
  • Adjusted EPS is flattered by about 0.06 to 0.08 EUR a year, because voluntary-leave charges are excluded from adjusted EBITDAaL every year (28.3 EURm in H1 2026 alone) while the savings from those exits are kept.
  • Working capital turned positive on public-sector receivables (716 EURm at the Q1 peak), although the H1 2026 build matched H1 2025's and is mostly seasonal.

The absences matter too. OTE has no medium-term targets, has held no capital markets day, makes no use of its balance sheet and has no tower plan. Its board sits at the legal minimum of three independent directors out of ten, and all board terms expire in 2027. The chief financial officer has served for 14 years, and the succession is untested.

Market view against mine. The market credits the change fully and has paid for it. I agree on the quality of execution but differ on what is left: the sell-side extrapolates FY2026's growth rate into FY2027 as if the change forces were still accelerating, when in fact they have matured. Pricing is the one internal change force still latent, and in my view the market under-appreciates it. The price clause now exists, covers about two million postpaid mobile and fixed contracts and recurs annually, while management's 2026 outlook assumes no further pricing; the December 2026 step is therefore a positive that the guidance does not include.

Where I differOTE's change forces have matured rather than accelerated; the one latent internal force is pricing, and the December 2026 price step is a positive that guidance does not yet include.

Strongest counter-case. A new leg of change could open: a capital markets day with numbered 2028 targets (about 25% probability within 18 months) or a monetisation of the towers. Neither has been announced.

What would change my view. Any numbered medium-term ambition; any change in Deutsche Telekom's stance on leverage; a change of chief financial officer.

Score: 55. A real, well-executed change that has largely run its course; the remaining internal forces are incremental, which puts OTE in the middle of the European pack on the strength of change.

#3Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Key messageOTE serves about half of Greek customers but earns nearly all of the industry's profit. Its retail moats widen with every fibre migration, but its wholesale moat is narrowing and its home market is small and slow.

Structure: Greece is a three-operator market in which OTE earns almost all of the profit. Three operators hold essentially 100% of Greek mobile and broadband subscribers, and OTE's two challengers rent 48% of their FTTH customers from OTE. The rivals cannot fund a price war and have raised prices with inflation two years running. Market conduct is cooperative: the operators divide fibre builds by territory, share sports content reciprocally and sign wholesale volume commitments with discounts of up to 28%, approved by the European Commission. PPC, the electricity company, is the only operator that put volume first, and its retail attack failed.

The structure's fragility is narrow and dated. The wholesale layer is exposed from 2027, and the ownership of both rivals is in play: United Group is exploring a sale of Nova, and Vodafone is under pressure from the investor Vega over its return on capital.

Business model and moats: OTE's retail moats widen with every fibre migration, but its wholesale moat is narrowing and its regulatory moats can be withdrawn. The moats are customer lock-in (70% of customers take bundles, and fibre needs in-building cabling), network quality (the fastest network in Greece ten years running on Ookla, and the only 5G Stand-Alone network), scale (65% of the market's revenue and 73% of its EBITDAaL), the cheapest capital in the market and Deutsche Telekom's procurement. The regulatory moats (the discount scheme, the copper stop-sell, the rural concession and the spectrum terms) are granted by the state and can be switched off by a decision. The wholesale host role is the one moat that is narrowing.

The size of the market is the limit. A 65% share of a 5 bn EUR market growing 2% to 4% a year in nominal terms allows only about 2% to 3% underlying revenue growth, and OTE's dominance rules out acquisitions in Greece.

Financial profile: OTE has the best financial profile in its peer set on every measure except growth. Returns on new capital are the one weak point: fibre costs about 500 EUR a line, earns about 10% more revenue per migrated customer and runs at 42% utilisation, so its returns stay low until copper is switched off and utilisation passes 50% to 60%.

Management: an above-average operator team working inside a frame set by Deutsche Telekom. The chief executive acts fast within the parent's frame, and the team is stable and well resourced. Communication is excellent on the quarter and thin on the medium term: OTE discloses no segment margins, no terms of its price clause and, until February, no basis for its payout. The culture is aligned around cash delivery, with pay tied to EBITDAaL and free cash flow, rather than being a source of advantage in itself. The 2022 to 2025 long-term incentive paid 252% of target, which raises a question about how its targets were calibrated.

Governance is the minimum standard for a controlled subsidiary: shareholders come first in cash and second in structure. The Chairman and CEO roles are combined; three of the ten directors are independent; related-party purchases total 572 EURm (16.5% of revenue); insiders hold almost no shares; and part of executive equity pay is in Deutsche Telekom shares.

Inference and so-what. For the forecast, this profile justifies stable retail share, a rising margin and near-certain cash delivery, but it justifies nothing above 2% to 3% revenue growth. For the valuation, it implies the multiple of a yield stock run by a disciplined, unadventurous capital allocator, not a compounder's multiple. OTE's buybacks are formulaic rather than price-sensitive: the 9.79m shares cancelled in June 2026 were bought at an average of 16.52 EUR.

Market view against mine. The market rates the structure and the balance sheet as I do, but it is more impressed than I am by management's ambition ("Europe's top digital telco", "AI-native by 2030"). That ambition is defensive, to be the best operator in a market OTE already dominates, and it carries no numbers. On one point I am more positive than the typical sceptic, for whom Telekom Austria at 8.1x is the worrying comparable: OTE's parent has shown that it passes cash through promptly, turning the proceeds of the Romanian sale into a special dividend within three months.

Strongest counter-case

Telekom Austria shows that a controlled, low-growth listed company can stay cheap for years. Like OTE, Telekom Austria is parent-controlled, has net cash, pays out heavily and guides reliably, yet it trades at 8.1x earnings with a 33% buy share. OTE's structure is closer to Telekom Austria's than to Swisscom's.

What would change my view. A sale of Nova to a volume-minded buyer would lower the structure score; a tower or leverage decision would raise the management score.

Score: 72. A near-monopoly profit pool under oligopoly conduct, the peer set's best margins, returns and balance sheet, and a capable operator team, held back from the top decile by a small, slow market, a narrowing wholesale moat, state-granted protections and minimum governance.

#4Conservative guidance, expectation management, and the record of delivery and upgrades

Key messageOTE meets its guidance precisely but never raises it during the year, and its next guide, in February 2027, is most likely to be set below the street.

Evidence: FY2026 guidance is on track. OTE set its FY2026 guide in February 2026, above the consensus of the time (+2.4% EBITDAaL growth), and reiterated it in May and July. H1 2026 delivered +2.9%, so H2 needs about +3.1%. For Q3, against a Q3 2025 base of 360.1 EURm, Morgan Stanley's preview has 366 EURm (+1.6%) and the model has 371 EURm (+3.0%).

The record on estimates: consensus rose once, with the February 2026 guide, and has since been flat, with a slight downward drift for the later years. Over twelve months consensus EPS is up 5.3% for FY2026 and 3.7% for FY2027; over six months it is down 0.8% for FY2026, 0.6% for FY2027 and 2.2% for FY2028.

Inference: OTE is an "honest tracker", which makes it valuable for predictability and worthless for upgrades. OTE guides to what the Deutsche Telekom budget will deliver and lands the number through cost timing, with voluntary exits and the phasing of operating costs giving it 10 to 15 EURm of flexibility. Its guidance is conservative in its assumptions (no further pricing in 2026; ICT described as "front-loaded") rather than in its number.

The next guide is the problem. I expect the FY2027 guide in February 2027 to be "about +1% to +2%" EBITDAaL growth (about 55% probability), "+2% to +3%" (30%) or flat (15%), against consensus at +2.7% to +3%. The next guidance event is therefore most likely a small negative for estimates, after which the company will meet whatever it has set.

Market view against mine. The sell-side reads OTE's guidance as a floor with upside, quoting management's own words that "the 2026 outlook is conservative", and carries +3% growth into 2027. I read the same words and reach the opposite conclusion for 2027: the conservatism in the 2026 guide was the price step that it did not assume, and in 2027 the company will have to assume a step just as ICT falls away. A guide of "about 2%" would be read as in line, because the market's own commentary already sits below the printed consensus; a guide of "about 1%" would not.

Strongest counter-case. Two careful brokers, Deutsche Bank (with the transit revenue removed) and Morgan Stanley, reach about +3% for FY2027. If management sees cost actions that I cannot see (the 2026 voluntary-leave scheme is the largest in years), a guide of +2% to +3% is possible and would hold consensus.

What would change my view. A tightening of the FY2026 guide to "at least 3%" at Q3; any statement on 30 October that the December price adjustment will be applied, and at what level.

Score: 52. Reliable, specific, one-year guidance from a company that meets it with precision and never raises it; the next guide is likely to be set below the street, so the upgrade record is absent while the delivery record is good.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Key messageOTE's operating leverage is high, but the revenue that carries it barely grows. The reliable multiplier is per share: the buyback and falling capex turn flat net income into 4% EPS growth and 8% growth in free cash flow per share.

Pricing power: real, but one year old and only nominal. After four years in which Greek consumer prices outran telecom prices by 25%, OTE applied a 2.6% CPI-linked price step in December 2025 to about two million postpaid contracts. The step was just under 1 EUR a month, bundled with extra data, and is worth about 20 to 24 EURm a year at about 95% margin, or about 1.5% of EBITDA. OTE also raised the minimum prepaid top-up from 13 to 15 EUR. Postpaid net additions then hit a 17-year high, so the price rise cost OTE no measurable loss of customers.

How the price clause works. The clause uses official Greek CPI over a twelve-month reference period, recurs annually, is written into each contract at signing and carries an undisclosed cap. Each point of price step is worth about 7 to 9 EURm of EBITDA. The model assumes a December 2026 step of about 3.7%, worth about 27 EURm of EBITDA in FY2027; without price rises, core EBITDA would fall about 0.6% to 0.9% a year in FY2027 and FY2028.

The one number that decides 2027The December 2026 price step, worth about 27 EURm of EBITDA, is larger than all of FY2027's forecast EBITDA growth.

The limits of OTE's pricing power.

  • The step shrinks as inflation falls: Telekom Austria's step fell from 7.8% to 2.9% in two years.
  • The clause covers postpaid contracts only, and 56% of OTE's mobile lines are prepaid.
  • OTE is subject to retail price controls as an operator with significant market power (SMP).
  • The step is politically exposed in a year of 5.1% inflation, 500 EURm of government cost-of-living support and street protests, although nothing in the files shows any Greek authority challenging it.

Operating leverage: high on core service revenue and almost nil on the rest, so group revenue is the wrong number to watch. Core service revenue (about 2.2 bn EUR, made up of mobile service, retail fixed and national wholesale revenue) carries an incremental margin of about 95% on price and 60% to 80% on volume. A 1% change in core service revenue is therefore worth about 19 EURm of EBITDA (1.3%) and about 2.2% of EBIT and EPS. Transit revenue (zero margin) and ICT revenue (15% to 20% margin) carry almost no leverage. The leverage also cuts the other way: 61% to 66% of cash operating costs are fixed (Jefferies), so 1% of cost inflation on about 1.1 bn EUR of controllable cost removes about 11 EURm of EBITDA.

The leverage below EBITDA that drove 2019 to 2025 is spent. EBIT margin rose from 8% to 24.5% over those years because D&A halved (from 1,138 to 582 EURm) while EBITDA stayed flat. D&A now creeps up, because capex of about 600 EURm runs above D&A and spectrum amortisation starts in 2028.

Financial leverage: nil in the base case, so the balance sheet's role is optionality. Net debt is 0.27x EBITDA, all at fixed rates and in euros, with interest cover above 20x. Refinancing the 0.875% bond at about 3% will cost about 10 EURm a year (about 1.2% of EPS), as a one-off step. At 1.5x brokers'-basis EBITDA, OTE could borrow about 1.9 bn EUR more, retire about a quarter of its shares and, after about 50 EURm of after-tax interest, add about 23% to EPS. Deutsche Telekom has called releveraging "unpalatable", so releveraging is a tail possibility, not a likely outcome.

Cost-out: a stabiliser that lets management land its guidance, not a growth driver. Gross savings are 25 to 30 EURm a year, from voluntary exits that pay back in the following year, digital deflection (online sales are 36% of gross additions) and copper switch-off from FY2028. Wage, services, energy and content inflation absorbs about two-thirds of those savings, so only about 8 EURm a year net reaches EBITDA. The larger cost lever is capex, which falls from about 600 EURm to about 560 EURm by FY2030, a saving worth about 8% to 9% of free cash flow.

Feedback loops: two reinforce OTE, one works against it from 2027, and two balance. The capital-return loop is the most dependable of the five, because free cash flow funds a buyback that adds about 3 points a year to EPS and DPS growth with near certainty. The loop against OTE runs through the Vodafone-PPC venture, and Nova is the tenant whose choice decides how fast it turns.

Inference and so-what: the per-share engine is dependable but modest, and it is the whole engine. Revenue growth does produce outsized profit growth at OTE, about 2x at the EPS line per unit of core service revenue, but core service revenue grows only about 1.5% a year, and almost all of that growth is price. The buyback and falling capex turn flat net income into 4% EPS growth and 8% growth in free cash flow per share.

Market view against mine. The market knows the buyback mechanism: Morgan Stanley attributes 3.2 of its 7.1 points of 2026 EPS growth to the buyback. What the market's narrative misses is that the other 4 points are not operating growth either (they come from changes of basis and one-off items), and that the D&A and interest tailwinds of the last six years are exhausted. One source describes D&A as in "continued decline" when it is flat.

Strongest counter-case. Copper switch-off savings could arrive two years early, although I doubt it, because the 2019 plan to close 17 exchanges was never implemented. Alternatively, OTE could add a flat-money price rise on top of indexation, which is the sector's durable form of pricing once inflation falls and which OTE has not yet used.

What would change my view. Confirmation that fixed contracts are included in the December step (worth about 10 EURm); a step at the September inflation rate of 5.1%; any sign that Deutsche Telekom would tolerate leverage of 1x EBITDA.

Score: 55. Strong operating leverage on a revenue base that barely grows, a dependable per-share loop, a contractual price mechanism that is real but shrinking, and a balance sheet whose power is deliberately unused.

#6Forecast financials: growth, margins and scope against the past

Key messageThe model has EBITDA growing about 1% a year after FY2026 and EPS about 4% a year, almost all from the buyback. The model sits below consensus from FY2027, the gap is widest at EBIT, and even the bull case for FY2027 only reaches consensus EPS.

What the forecast says, in four lines.

  • Revenue falls 5.5% in FY2027, but the fall carries no information, because about 390 EURm of transit and ICT revenue leaves with almost no EBITDA.
  • EBITDA grows 3% in FY2026 and then about 1% a year, as price rises and gross efficiency gains outweigh the decline in national wholesale revenue and cost inflation (first panel below).
  • Net income is flat (633 to 652 EURm), because D&A rises about 1.3% a year and interest costs step up once.
  • EPS rises 17% over four years, of which about 13 points come from the falling share count and about 3 points from profit; free cash flow per share rises about 8% a year from 2027 as capex falls and working capital is released.
The engineEPS growth of about 4% a year comes almost entirely from the buyback: net income is flat because the D&A and interest tailwinds that lifted EBIT from 272 to 849 EURm between FY2019 and FY2025 are exhausted.

Against the past: the forecast is better than FY2019 to FY2025 on EBITDA and cash per share, but much worse on EBIT and net income. EBITDA grows about 1% a year against flat; EPS grows about 4% a year against about 3%; EBIT and net income are flat against strong growth, because the D&A and interest tailwinds are gone. The EBITDA margin rises about 3.5 points to FY2028, but about 3 of those points are the arithmetic of removing zero-margin revenue; genuine operating leverage adds only about half a point.

Scope for double-digit growth: none without a capital decision. No plausible operating case delivers double-digit growth in EBITDA or net income. EPS growth reaches high single digits only with a full pass-through of the tax windfall into buybacks, or with a price step of 4% or more on fixed and mobile contracts. Double-digit EPS growth requires a capital decision: releveraging would add 20% to 25% to EPS in one step.

My own view of the inputs: I keep every input in the model, and the skew within my range is mildly upward. My central view of FY2027 EBITDAaL growth is +1% to +1.5%, and the model sits at the low end of that range. Two refinements would move the model, and they offset each other: the Bank of Greece's 3.1% CPI projection points to a price step nearer 3.0% than 3.7% (about -5 EURm of EBITDA), while the larger 2026 voluntary-leave scheme pays back (about +5 to +10 EURm). Against consensus, the model is 2% lower on FY2027 EBITDA and 6% lower on FY2028 EPS, and I would defend both gaps.

The range of outcomes is narrow for FY2026 and FY2027 and widens after.

  • FY2026: EBITDAaL within plus or minus 1% of 1,415 EURm, with about 90% probability.
  • FY2027: EBITDAaL of 1,393 to 1,458 EURm (-1.5% to +3.0%), EPS of 1.57 to 1.72 EUR and a distribution of 560 to 620 EURm (table below).
  • FY2028 to FY2030: a fat left tail from the wholesale loop (a fast migration by Nova would take a further 2% off EBITDA by FY2030) and a right tail from capital decisions.

Market view against mine: consensus extrapolates 2026 into 2027 and implies net income growth that the drivers do not support. For FY2027, consensus has EBITDA +2.7%, revenue +1.9% and EPS +3.8%, followed by EPS +6.5% in FY2028. Consensus has not removed the transit revenue: brokers' FY2027 revenue forecasts range from 3,383 to 3,622 EURm, a 7% spread that is explained entirely by how each broker treats transit and ICT. Consensus also carries D&A rising only 1.3% a year while capex runs above D&A, and it implies net income growth of 4% to 5% a year. I agree with consensus on FY2026, on the direction of the dividend and on capex falling.

Strongest counter-case: the disagreement with consensus is about EBIT, not the share count. One of the three independent analyses behind this memo observes that consensus EPS embeds little buyback accretion: consensus net income divided by consensus EPS implies about 382m shares in FY2027, against 381m on the buyback path, which falls to 370m in FY2028. If consensus EBIT were right, EPS would therefore be 1.74 to 1.76 EUR.

What would change my view. Q3 2026 mobile service revenue growth below 2% (which would lower the core); FY2027 System Solutions revenue above 580 EURm (which would raise ICT); the February guide.

Score: 35. Highly predictable forecasts of a slow-growing cash machine: EBITDA about +1%, EPS about +4% (all buyback), free cash flow per share about +8%; no scope for double-digit profit growth without a capital decision, and margins that rise mainly by arithmetic.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Key messageOver the next year, consensus FY2027 EPS is three times as likely to be cut as raised (about 60% against about 20%). The December price step and the February guide are the whole of the 18-month case.

Evidence and inference: the calendar holds one positive that guidance excludes, the December price step, followed by one probable estimate cut, the February 2027 guide. The table below the calendar sizes the consensus changes that I expect the calendar to bring.

The decisive point: even the bull case produces a held consensus, not an upgrade cycle, because consensus already sits at the bull case. The bull case is a 4% price step on mobile and fixed contracts with ICT revenue held flat by RRF spill-over, which gives FY2027 EBITDAaL growth of +3%, exactly where consensus is.

The market's narrative knows the bull shape of the story but not its arithmetic. The bull shape is a clean Greek cash yield, a Greek re-rating and PPC defeated. The arithmetic is a flat core, an EPS line that is all buyback and a year that depends on one December decision. What the market learns over the next two sets of results is therefore mostly negative. The two narrative positives that the market under-rates, the durability of Greek indexation and the decline in capex after 2027, will be recognised slowly and do not show in near-term numbers.

The decisive pointThe December step and the February guide are the whole of the 18-month case: the December step is the only positive that guidance excludes, and the February guide is most likely to be set below the street.

Market view against mine. The street's mean target price (20.92 EUR, +10%) and median Buy rating imply modest upside with estimates intact. I expect similar modest upside, but from a lower estimate base and a higher multiple, which is a different and less comfortable path.

Strongest counter-case. If management names the December step and its size on the Q3 call, or signals "+2% to +3%" for 2027, the February cut would come forward and shrink to nothing. A first set of numbered medium-term targets would be a narrative positive even if the numbers were conservative.

What would change my view. Either of those signals on the Q3 call; or H2 2026 System Solutions revenue well above the model's 313 EURm.

Score: 30. The next six to twelve months carry more estimate risk than estimate reward: a guide below the street, a consensus cut once, and a narrative that has to absorb a flat core, with the dividend line the only one likelier to rise.

#8Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative and price, and at peers

Key messageOTE's price momentum is intact but fading, its estimate momentum has stalled with a cut ahead, and Telekom Austria and Orange Polska have taken over as the sector's upgrade stories.

Evidence: Viewforth's Master Dashboard on 27 October 2026.

Peers: the sector's revision momentum is mixed. The Polish and Austrian names are being upgraded on cost savings and growth in Central and Eastern Europe, while the Nordic names and Elisa are being cut.

Inference: OTE's momentum is following a sentiment-first, numbers-second sequence, and the numbers step is due in February. Price momentum is intact but ageing: the shares are in a three-month drawdown inside a twelve-month uptrend. Estimate momentum has stalled. Narrative momentum has turned from "new OTE" to "watch the venture". Among peers, OTE is no longer the upgrade story it was in early 2026; Orange Polska and Telekom Austria have taken over that role.

Market view against mine. I agree with the market on direction, and I add one observation: the three-month fall coincided with the cut in Viewforth's country tilt for Greece to Neutral (9 October) and with risk-off in European sovereign bonds, not with OTE news. That timing confirms that Greek flows set OTE's multiple.

What would change my view. A Q3 beat with a named December step would reverse the sell-side momentum; a break below the 200-day average would reverse the technical momentum.

Score: 42. Price momentum intact but fading, estimate and narrative momentum stalled with a cut ahead, and peers that have overtaken OTE as the sector's upgrade stories.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Key messageOTE's earnings are among the simplest and most predictable in European telecoms, within about plus or minus 3% on FY2027 EBITDA. The share price carries a range about six times as wide, because Greece, not OTE, sets the multiple.

Simplicity: the forecast turns on three nameable variables and one capital decision, and nothing else. The three variables are the December price step, the ICT roll-off and the speed of wholesale migration; the capital decision is the use of the tax windfall. Below EBITDA everything is mechanical (fixed-rate debt, a 23.5% tax rate, no minority interests, a formula buyback), which is why the model's EPS matched the Analyst's to within 0.01 EUR in every year. Three independent sets of analysis converged on the same three variables from about fifty separate judgements and six research reports.

The key judgements, with the arithmetic (FY2027 unless stated; EPS base 1.66 EUR on about 381m shares; tax rate 23.5%).

  1. The December 2026 price step (model 3.7%, about 27 EURm of EBITDA). Each 1 point of step is worth about 7 EURm of EBITDA, about 5.4 EURm of net income and about 0.014 EUR of EPS (0.9%). A step of 2% instead of 3.7% cuts EBITDA by 12 EURm, EBITDAaL growth from +1.0% to +0.2% and EPS by 0.025 EUR (-1.5%). No step cuts EBITDA by 27 EURm, turns EBITDAaL growth to -0.9% for the year, cuts EPS by 0.054 EUR (-3.3%) and removes the narrative's one positive. A step of 4.5% that also covers fixed contracts adds 10 EURm of EBITDA and 0.02 EUR of EPS. The probability of a step of at least 3% is about 70%.
  2. Wholesale migration to the venture (model: national wholesale revenue -6% in FY2027 and -8% a year after, about -51 EURm of EBITDA by FY2030). Each 10% of national wholesale revenue (about 23 EURm at an 85% margin) is worth about 20 EURm of EBITDA and about 0.04 EUR of EPS (2.4%). In the bear case, Nova follows Vodafone onto the venture after a sale, and national wholesale revenue falls 15% to 20% a year from FY2028: FY2028 revenue is about 15 to 25 EURm below the base case, EBITDA about 15 to 20 EURm lower and EPS 0.03 to 0.04 EUR lower (about -2%); by FY2030 revenue is about 100 EURm lower and EBITDAaL about 3.5% lower than in the base case. In the fast-defection tail, both rivals leave within two to three years, costing 60 to 100 EURm of EBITDA (-4% to -7%), with a retail price response on top. I put the plausibility of that tail at 10% to 15%.
  3. The multiple. Two-year-forward EPS at December 2027 is 1.80 EUR, so each 1.0x of multiple is worth 1.80 EUR per share, about 9.5% of the price: 12.5x gives 22.5 EUR, 11.5x gives 20.7 EUR, 10.3x (the five-year median) gives 18.5 EUR and 9.1x (the five-year low) gives 16.4 EUR. The multiple is the widest source of uncertainty in the case, and Greece sets it, not OTE.
  4. The System Solutions roll-off (model -15% in FY2027, to 521 EURm, at a 15% to 20% margin). Each 10% of System Solutions revenue (about 60 EURm) is worth about 10 EURm of EBITDA and about 0.02 EUR of EPS. A 30% fall would cost a further 15 to 18 EURm of EBITDA (EPS -0.03 EUR, -2%); a flat year would add the same amount. The undisclosed margin is the fragility: if the margin is 25% rather than 17%, the same revenue fall costs half as much again.
  5. Capital policy. A full pass-through of the windfall (a 740 EURm distribution in 2027 rather than 585 EURm) would buy about 7.5m more shares at about 20.5 EUR, cutting the FY2028 share count by 2% and adding about 0.03 to 0.04 EUR to FY2028 EPS. Releveraging to 1.5x EBITDA would add about 0.35 to 0.40 EUR (about 23%). I put the probability of the pass-through within 18 months at about 15%, and of releveraging at low single digits.
  6. A sixth, quieter judgement: D&A. The model has D&A rising 1.3% a year. If D&A rose 4% a year (the adverse case), FY2028 D&A would be about 640 EURm against 612 EURm, EBIT 28 EURm lower and EPS 0.06 EUR lower (-3.4%), and run-rate EPS growth would fall to about 2%.

Suddenness, predictability and trackability: OTE's disclosure tracks outcomes well and drivers poorly, so the first hard evidence on 2027 arrives in February 2027. OTE discloses no ICT margin or backlog, no cap in its price clause, no contract terms and, until February, no payout basis.

Price risks, justified or not, are larger than the fundamental risks and rising. A 10% to 15% fall in the shares with no change in the company is plausible, but the dividend yield (5.5% at 17 EUR, 6.1% at 15.5 EUR) and the buyback put a floor under the price. The price risks come from four sources:

  • Rates: telecoms trade as yield stocks, with the US 10-year yield near 5.1% and the ECB expected to raise rates.
  • Country: Greek sovereign spreads, and Viewforth's country tilt for Greece, which has been cut to Neutral.
  • Index transition: OTE's pro-forma weight is 0.02% of MSCI Europe, against 0.25% of MSCI EM Eastern Europe, and the net passive inflow is about 63m USD, about six days' volume. The stock fell 6% in January 2026 on doubts about inclusion, and after Greece's 2001 upgrade the Greek market underperformed for 10 to 11 months.
  • Liquidity: a free float of 36.6% and 8 to 11m USD of daily trading.

Sector and cyclicality: connectivity is non-discretionary, so the precedents that matter are structural rather than cyclical. OTE's revenue moved within -1% to +4% a year through the energy shock and the pandemic. Four structural precedents are relevant:

  • Telecom Italia against Open Fiber: a decade of wholesale erosion, ending in rationalisation.
  • BT against the UK's alternative fibre networks: Openreach cut wholesale prices and locked in volume, which is OTE's playbook.
  • Vodafone Germany: a 1.1 bn EUR loss of EBITDAaL.
  • The Iliad and Digi mobile entries in France, Italy and Spain: Digi cut Spanish postpaid ARPU by 9.8%. Greece has no fourth mobile network, and PPC has repeatedly ruled one out.

The Greek sovereign is the tail risk. OTE traded at 6x earnings in 2012 and at 3x EBITDA at the trough, and Deutsche Bank's devaluation case values the shares at 5.70 EUR. The risk is remote, but it is the one risk that a one-country company cannot diversify.

Market view against mine. The market's list of risks centres on PPC and takes account of the sovereign; my list centres on the price step for 2027 and on the venture for 2028 to 2030, with the multiple as the real source of uncertainty. I think the range of fundamental outcomes is narrower than the sell-side's bear-to-bull range (Morgan Stanley's 1.23 to 1.85 EUR of EPS includes price wars that I do not expect within 18 months), and that the range of share prices is wider than the sell-side's targets (17.50 to 23.80 EUR) suggest.

Strongest counter-case. Concentration cuts both ways: with no diversification among the drivers, a capped price step alone would take FY2027 EBITDAaL growth from +1% to -1%, and nothing else in the model would offset it within a year except cost timing.

What would change my view. A Hellenic Competition Commission decision that names Nova as a tenant of the venture; a Greek government statement on telecom indexation; an EETT move on the discount scheme.

Score: 62. Among the simplest and most predictable earnings in European telecoms (three drivers, a mechanical P&L below EBITDA, a range of plus or minus 3% on FY2027 EBITDA), carrying a wider-than-average price range because the multiple is set by Greek flows and sovereign risk rather than by the company.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Key messageOTE's fundamentals are reinforcing while its expectations are stalling, and the way the market absorbs the February 2027 reset will decide the stock's next phase.

Evidence: the three lifecycle readings disagree with each other, and the disagreement is the point. The dashboard's rule assigns the stock to "Turning/Inflecting", because the price is above a rising 200-day average and technical momentum is graded B. The underlying readings differ:

  • Fundamentals are in a steady reinforcing phase: the cash return is compounding, the margin is rising, the buyback is mechanical and the change programme has delivered.
  • Expectations are at the end of the 2025 to 2026 re-rating and about to absorb a reset of 2027 numbers: the buy share is down 15 points, estimates are flat and a guide below the street is due.
  • The price has moved from 9x to 11x earnings as the PPC fear cleared, the Romanian exit completed, the payout policy was codified and Greece re-rated, and it has stalled for three months as European markets turned risk-off.

Inference: on the six-stage lifecycle vocabulary, OTE is "reinforcing" in its fundamentals and "stalling" in its expectations, with the price between the two. OTE is not bottoming, because the multiple is at the 69th percentile of its five-year range. It is not collapsing, because an 8% cash yield and an almost unlevered balance sheet do not collapse. It is no longer turning up, because that phase was 2025.

The setupThe setup Richard wants (a cause for concern clearing in a high-quality business on a multiple in the bottom quartile of its history) was crisp in 2025 and is likelier to re-form after February 2027 than it is to be available today.

Market view against mine. Morgan Stanley's "A New OTE" framing is a "thesis broadening" call. I think the broadening (pure-play status, the payout policy, the Greek re-rating) is complete, and that the thesis is now narrowing to cash yield plus the debate about the venture. The dashboard's "Turning/Inflecting" label is a reading of the price and overstates the fundamental phase.

Strongest counter-case. A capital markets day, a tower move or releveraging would reopen "thesis broadening"; a sale of Nova to a maverick buyer would start a genuine "stalling" phase in the fundamentals.

What would change my view. The February 2027 guide and the market's reaction to it; MSCI's pricing window in April 2027.

Score: 45. A stock whose fundamentals are reinforcing and whose expectations are stalling, past its turning-up phase, with the next leg contingent on absorbing an estimate reset; an average lifecycle position for the sector, better than it looks on the fundamentals and worse than it looks on the price chart.

#11The fair multiple

Key messageMy fair multiple for OTE is 11.5x to 12.0x two-year-forward earnings. The guideline 12.5x is a destination over two to three years, not a fair level for the next six months.

The guideline. Viewforth's Phases guideline sets 12.5x for a stock in the "Turning/Inflecting" phase. For OTE, 12.5x is the 60th percentile of the ten-year range of two-year-forward P/E and 13% above today's 11.05x.

My view: 11.5x to 12.0x, for four reasons.

  1. The ten-year range is the wrong anchor for OTE. OTE traded at 13x to 18x in 2016 to 2019, when interest rates were near zero and EPS grew at double digits as D&A halved and the EBIT margin rose from 8% to 24%. That tailwind is spent, and the Greek ten-year bond now yields 4.33%. Since mid-2022 the stock has not traded above 12.4x, and since 2023 not above 11.4x (reached in July 2026); the five-year median is 10.3x and the five-year 75th percentile is 11.0x.
  2. The lifecycle phase does not justify a premium. The fundamentals are reinforcing but the expectations are stalling, and the guideline rule itself says to set a lower multiple for the stalling and turning-up phases, where forecasts are less certain. The next two catalysts are estimate cuts.
  3. No sector tide will carry the multiple to 12.5x. OTE's multiple is driven by the company and the country, not the sector. Only a Greek re-rating, MSCI inclusion and OTE's own cash steps can lift it, and OTE is smoothing its cash steps rather than spiking them.
  4. The comparables bracket the range. Telekom Austria (parent-controlled, net cash, high payout, slow growth) trades at 8.1x; KPN (full cash return, with 80% of its market value returned over five years) at 14.3x; and the European sector median is 11.8x, at the 34th percentile of its own history. At 11.5x to 12.0x, OTE sits about a point below the sector's historical level, reflecting a cleaner balance sheet and a slower growth rate. That is where a 4% EPS grower with an 8% cash yield belongs when the risk-free rate is 4%.

What 12.5x needs. Two to three of the four conditions below are plausible by mid-2027, which is why I treat 12.5x as a destination over two to three years rather than as a fair level for the next six months.

Sensitivity. Each 0.5x of multiple is worth 0.90 EUR on the December 2027 share price (about 4.7%): the price is 20.7 EUR at 11.5x, 21.6 EUR at 12.0x and 22.5 EUR at 12.5x.

Market view against mine. Morgan Stanley's 23.80 EUR target is about 13x its 2028 EPS and assumes that OTE's 37% EV/EBITDA discount to the sector closes as Greece re-rates. Barclays' 18.00 EUR Sell rating is a valuation call based on the highest FY2026 EPS in the set (1.84 EUR, including the tax one-off). I sit between the two: the discount to the sector is partly structural (a controlled float, no growth lever, a Greek country premium) and partly closable (the A- rating, MSCI inclusion, contractual pricing).

Strongest counter-case. The sector note finds that cash gains already in management's hands (contractual price rises, capex falling on an owned network, cost cuts forced by an owner) are rewarded with premium multiples, and OTE has all three. The re-rating could also run further than the five-year history suggests if Greek active ownership broadens: only 12% of European active long-only funds hold any Greek equity.

What would change my view. Greek ten-year yields back below 3.5%; a tower or leverage decision; a sale of Nova to a maverick buyer (which would lower my fair multiple to 10x).

Score: 45. The guideline 12.5x is above my 11.5x to 12.0x: it is a level the stock has earned only in zero-rate, double-digit-growth years, and the near-term catalysts argue for the lower end of the phase range rather than the higher.

#12Total shareholder return, by the DuPont split

Key messageAt my fair multiple, the shares return about +19% to +24% to December 2027; cash and the buyback alone deliver a high-single-digit return a year, so the re-rating is the upside, not the requirement. The downside to the trough band of multiples is 8% to 15%.

The model's return at the guideline 12.5x.

Read like for like, the return is one-third cash, two-fifths re-rating and one-fifth earnings.

  1. The 24.45 EUR value per share at December 2027 is a 22.47 EUR share price plus 1.98 EUR of dividends (the FY2026 and FY2027 dividends of 0.95 and 1.03 EUR).
  2. The 22.47 EUR price is 12.5x the model's December 2027 two-year-forward EPS of 1.80 EUR (FY2029 EPS).
  3. Over the fourteen months to December 2027 (the template's "18-month" column), the return is therefore about 10 points of cash, about 12 points from the multiple (11.2x today to 12.5x: +11.6%) and about 6 points from growth in two-year-forward EPS (about 1.70 EUR today to 1.80 EUR: +5.9%). These legs compound to +18.1% in the price and +28.5% in total.
  4. The three-year return tells the same story with a bigger cash leg (3.05 EUR of dividends, 16 points), the same re-rating and about 13 points of earnings growth (two-year-forward EPS of about 1.93 EUR by mid-2029).

At my fair multiple, the return is still attractive for the risk. At 12.0x the December 2027 share price is 21.6 EUR and the total return about +24%; at 11.5x, 20.7 EUR and about +19%; at an unchanged 11.2x, 20.2 EUR and about +16% (6 points from earnings, 10 from cash). Over three years at 11.5x to 12.0x, the total return is about +32% to +37%, or about 11% to 12.5% a year, of which the cash leg alone contributes 16 points.

Downside: 8% to 15% on unchanged earnings, and about 20% in the bear case. At the five-year 25th-percentile multiple (9.85x) on unchanged earnings, the share price would be 17.6 EUR (-8%); at the five-year low (9.09x), 16.2 EUR (-15%). A trough multiple combined with a 5% earnings cut (the wholesale-and-ICT bear case) gives about 15 EUR (-20%). At those prices the dividend yield is 5.4% to 6.3%.

Market view against mine. The sell-side's mean target (20.92 EUR) plus a 5% yield implies about +15% over twelve months on intact estimates. My +19% to +24% to December 2027 comes instead from lower estimates, a larger cash leg and a modest re-rating. The cash leg is larger because the 2027 distribution is smoothed up to about 585 EURm, against the 560 EURm implied by a consensus DPS of 0.94 EUR. We agree that the return is cash-heavy; I differ on the sequence, which runs through an estimate cut first.

Strongest counter-case, in both directions. If Greek active ownership broadens after May 2027 and migration to the venture is slow, the stock could trade back to its 2022 band (13x to 13.7x), and the 18-month return would exceed 35%. If instead the February 2027 guide meets a risk-off European market, the whole 2026 re-rating (from 10x to 11x) could reverse before the cash leg accrues.

What would change my view. The drivers of the multiple listed in #11; the December price step and the February guide.

Score: 55. A cash-heavy return (about 8% a year from dividends and buybacks before any re-rating) with 6 to 12 points of multiple upside to a fair level and 8% to 15% of multiple downside to the trough band; attractive for the risk, but not the unusually skewed earnings-and-upgrade return Richard looks for.

#13Summary conclusion

The conclusionOTE is a very good business whose shares are likely to be cheaper to buy after February 2027 than today, unless the Q3 call names a December price step of 3.5% or more.

OTE is a very good business in a small market. It is run well inside its parent's frame and returns all its cash; its earnings are among the most predictable in European telecoms; and its share price is set by Greece rather than by the company.

Over the next 12 to 24 months, the investment case has three parts:

  • A cash-yield compounder: about 8% a year in dividends and buybacks; EPS growth of about 4% a year, almost all from the falling share count; and growth in free cash flow per share of about 8% a year from 2027 as capex falls.
  • Plus a re-rating option on the falling Greek equity premium and MSCI inclusion.
  • Minus a near-term estimate reset in February 2027.

Three facts shape the timing, and none of them breaks the case. Without the price step and the public ICT boom, the core business is flat; FY2027 depends on one December pricing decision; and the first credible attack on the wholesale layer that carries OTE's excess return arrives in H1 2027, slowly and within limits. Together, these facts say that the shares will be cheaper to buy after February 2027 than today.

Four events could change that sequence: a 4% price step on fixed and mobile contracts, a "+2% to +3%" guide for FY2027, a numbered medium-term ambition, or a tower or leverage decision. Each is plausible, and none has been announced.
